questions.prompt: Rice A and B cost ₹30 and ₹90 per kg; pulses C and D cost ₹100 and ₹120 per kg. Buy at least 1 kg each of A and B and 0.5 kg each of C and D. Find the minimum and maximum costs of 5 kg.

Allocate every remaining kilogram to the cheapest item for the minimum and the costliest item for the maximum.
questions.solution: The compulsory 3 kg costs $30+90+0.5(100)+0.5(120)=230$. There are 2 kg left. The cheapest choice adds $2(30)=60$, giving ₹290. The costliest adds $2(120)=240$, giving ₹470. Both allocations satisfy every lower bound. Hence **C**.
questions.theory: For a linear cost $\sum c_i x_i$ with $x_i\ge l_i$ and $\sum x_i=W$, write $x_i=l_i+z_i$. Then $z_i\ge0$ and $\sum z_i=R=W-\sum l_i$. The variable cost is a weighted average of the coefficients times $R$, so it lies between $R\min c_i$ and $R\max c_i$. These bounds are attained by putting all excess mass in an extremal item. Check feasibility $W\ge\sum l_i$ first. Upper limits on quantities would require allocating the remainder in price order rather than all to one item.

similar_questions.solution: The compulsory cost is ₹70 and 2 kg remain. The range is ₹110–₹170.

similar_questions.prompt: When is the minimum unique?
similar_questions.solution: If the cheapest coefficient is unique and positive remainder is available, all remainder must go to that item. Equal cheapest prices give multiple minima.

questions.prompt: A square board is divided into 9 equal squares. Three independent uniformly random shots hit the board. What is the probability that at least two hit the same small square?
hints: Use the complementary event: all three shots hit different squares.
The second shot must avoid one square; the third must avoid two.
questions.solution: All distinct has probability $1\cdot(8/9)\cdot(7/9)=56/81$. The requested event is its complement: $1-56/81=25/81$. **C**. The assumptions are independent shots and equal hit probabilities for all nine squares.
questions.theory: The occupancy or birthday calculation for $k$ independent choices among $m$ equally likely cells is $P(\text{all distinct})=(m)_k/m^k$ for $k\le m$, where $(m)_k=m(m-1)\cdots(m-k+1)$. At least one collision is its complement. For $k>m$, collision is certain by the pigeonhole principle. Exactly one pair and at least one pair are different events when $k\ge4$. With unequal cell probabilities, the simple product formula no longer applies.

similar_questions.solution: There are 9 choices for the shared square, each with probability $(1/9)^3$, so the result is $1/81$.

questions.prompt: Clock A loses 4 minutes per real hour; C gains 3 minutes per real hour. Both agree with the correct clock at Monday 8 pm. When C reads Wednesday 2 pm, what does A read?

questions.solution: Because $f$ is bounded and integer-valued, its tail extrema stabilise at integers: the largest and smallest values occurring infinitely often. Thus A and B hold. Since $f(n)+n\to+\infty$, its liminf and limsup are both $+\infty$ in the extended real line. Infinity is not a natural number, so C is false and D is true. **C**.
questions.theory: For a real sequence, $\limsup a_n=\lim_{N\to\infty}\sup_{n\ge N}a_n$ and similarly for infimum. These limits can be infinite. A bounded sequence need not converge, but its liminf and limsup are finite and equal exactly when it converges. questions.prompt: Which statement about continuous maps $\mathbb R^2\to\mathbb R$ is true?

options.A: At most countably many continuous maps
options.B: At most finitely many continuous surjections

hints: Constant maps disprove the first claim; shifted coordinate projections disprove the second.
Restrict a proposed injection to a circle and use compactness and connectedness.
questions.solution: Every real constant gives a different continuous map, so A is false. The maps $(x,y)\mapsto x+c$ are distinct continuous surjections, so B is false. Suppose an injection existed. Its restriction to $S^1$ is a continuous injection from a compact space into a Hausdorff space, hence a homeomorphism onto its image. The image is a nondegenerate compact interval in $\mathbb R$. Removing an interior point disconnects that interval, while removing one point from $S^1$ leaves a connected space. Contradiction. No continuous injection exists, so C is false and **D** holds.
questions.theory: A continuous bijection is not automatically a homeomorphism. It is one if its domain is compact and target Hausdorff, because compact sets have closed images. Connected subsets of the real line are intervals. Removing a point can distinguish topological spaces: a circle minus one point is homeomorphic to a line, while an interval minus an interior point has two components. Restricting a proposed map to a convenient compact subset often turns a difficult global problem into a topological invariant argument. Set-theoretic bijections between R and R² do exist; continuity is the obstruction here.

similar_questions.prompt: Can there be a continuous injection from a circle into the line?
similar_questions.solution: No. Its compact connected image would be an interval homeomorphic to the circle, contradicted by puncturing at an interior image point.

similar_questions.prompt: Give a continuous surjection from R² to R.
similar_questions.solution: The projection $(x,y)\mapsto x$ is continuous and surjective.

questions.prompt: For which domain does $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^n\sin(nx)/n^{\log_e n}$ converge uniformly?
hints: Bound $|\sin(nx)|$ independently of x.
For sufficiently large n, $\log n\ge2$.
questions.solution: For all real x, $|(-1)^n\sin(nx)/n^{\log n}|\le n^{-\log n}$. For $n\ge\lceil e^2\rceil$, $n^{-\log n}\le n^{-2}$. The majorant series converges, and finitely many initial terms do not affect convergence. The Weierstrass M-test gives absolute and uniform convergence on the entire real line. **D**.
questions.theory: The M-test: if $|f_n(x)|\le M_n$ for every x in a domain and $\sum M_n<\infty$, then $\sum f_n$ converges uniformly and absolutely there. Uniform convergence controls tails simultaneously for every x; pointwise convergence alone does not. Here $n^{-\log n}=\exp[-(\log n)^2]$ eventually decays faster than any fixed power $n^{-p}$. The alternating sign is unnecessary because an absolute majorant already works. A uniformly convergent sum of continuous functions is continuous; termwise differentiation requires additional conditions on derivatives.

questions.prompt: For an arbitrary real sequence $(a_n)$, which assertion always holds?

options.D: Some b and subsequence make $\sum|b-a_{n_k}/(1+|a_{n_k}|)|$ converge

hints: The transformed sequence $b_n=a_n/(1+|a_n|)$ is bounded.
After finding a convergent subsequence, select an even faster one with error at most 2⁻ᵏ.
questions.solution: Put $b_n=a_n/(1+|a_n|)$, so $|b_n|<1$. By Bolzano–Weierstrass, some subsequence converges to a real b. Thin it further to ensure $|b-b_{n_k}|<2^{-k}$. Therefore the nonnegative series in D is bounded by a convergent geometric series. A fails for $a_n=(-1)^n$, giving constant terms 1/2. B fails for $a_n=1$. For C, again take $a_n=(-1)^n$: the term magnitudes alternate between $|b-1/2|$ and $|b+1/2|$ and cannot both tend to zero. **D**.
questions.theory: Every bounded real sequence has a convergent subsequence. Given convergence to b and any positive summable error sequence ε_k, choose increasing indices n_k with distance below ε_k. This strengthens subsequential convergence to summability along a further subsequence. It does not force convergence of a series of the values themselves: those may approach a nonzero limit. For every convergent series, its individual terms must tend to zero. Alternating signs alone never guarantee convergence; the standard alternating-series test also needs magnitudes decreasing to zero.

similar_questions.prompt: Show every bounded real sequence has a subsequence whose successive differences are absolutely summable.
similar_questions.solution: Choose a subsequence with $|b_{n_k}-b|<2^{-k}$. Then $|b_{n_{k+1}}-b_{n_k}|\le2^{-(k+1)}+2^{-k}$, a summable bound.

similar_questions.prompt: Must every convergent sequence have summable errors from its limit?
similar_questions.solution: No: $1/n\to0$, but $\sum1/n$ diverges. A thinner subsequence $n_k=2^k$ has summable errors.

questions.prompt: An n×n matrix A has exactly r distinct nonzero eigenvalues. Which assertion is always true?

questions.solution: Choose one eigenvector for each distinct nonzero eigenvalue. They are independent and all lie in im A, so its dimension, rank A, is at least r. **C**. A fails for A=I₂ (rank 2, r=1). B fails for a nilpotent Jordan block of rank n−1. D fails for diag(1,−1), whose square is I₂ and merges the two eigenvalues.
questions.theory: The rank is the dimension of the image, while nullity is the dimension of the kernel; their sum is n. Distinct eigenvalues give independent eigenvectors, but eigenvalue multiplicities and Jordan blocks mean that the number of distinct eigenvalues does not determine rank. All eigenvalues zero implies nilpotence over a field in which the characteristic polynomial splits, not the zero matrix. Polynomial functions of a matrix map eigenvalues through the polynomial; distinct values may collide, as λ and −λ do under squaring.

questions.prompt: For arbitrary 2×2 matrices A and B, which determinant identity holds?
hints: The determinant of a 2×2 matrix is quadratic in its entries.

questions.solution: Write $A=(a_{ij})$, $B=(b_{ij})$. Expanding gives $\det(A+B)=\det A+\det B+M$, where $M=a_{11}b_{22}+b_{11}a_{22}-a_{12}b_{21}-b_{12}a_{21}$. Replacing B by −B changes M to −M and leaves det B unchanged. Adding gives $2\det A+2\det B$. **C**.
questions.theory: The determinant is multilinear in columns, but is not linear as a function of the whole matrix. In dimension two it is a homogeneous quadratic form and satisfies the parallelogram identity Q(u+v)+Q(u−v)=2Q(u)+2Q(v). The degree matters: in general det(cA)=cⁿdet(A), and this particular identity need not hold in other dimensions. Expanding a polynomial and cancelling odd mixed terms is a useful method for matrix identities.

questions.prompt: An iid sample has pdf $f(x\mid\theta)=(\log\theta)\theta^x/(\theta-1)$ for 0<x<1, θ>1. Classify $T=\sum X_i$.

questions.solution: Let η=log θ>0. The joint density is $[\eta/(e^\eta-1)]^n\exp(\eta T)\mathbf1_{(0,1)^n}$. Factorization makes T sufficient. This is a full one-parameter exponential family with fixed support and natural parameter space containing an open interval, so its natural statistic T is complete. Hence **C**. The likelihood ratio for two sample points is parameter-independent exactly when their sums agree, also showing minimal sufficiency.
questions.theory: A statistic is sufficient when the likelihood factors into a data-only part and a part depending on the data through that statistic. It is complete if Eθ[g(T)]=0 for every θ implies g(T)=0 almost surely for every θ, whenever those expectations exist. Full exponential families with parameter-independent support and a natural parameter space containing a nonempty open set have complete natural statistics. Completeness is not automatic for curved families or arbitrary sufficient statistics. Combined with sufficiency, it supports unique unbiased estimators via the Lehmann–Scheffé theorem.

questions.prompt: One observation has logistic location pdf $f(x\mid\theta)=e^{x-\theta}/(1+e^{x-\theta})^2$. Find a UMP size-α test of H₀:θ≤θ₀ versus H₁:θ>θ₀.

questions.solution: For θ₁>θ₀, the derivative of the log likelihood ratio with respect to x is $2[s(x-\theta_0)-s(x-\theta_1)]>0$, where $s(u)=e^u/(1+e^u)$. Thus the family has monotone likelihood ratio in X. The upper-tail test is most powerful for every θ₁>θ₀ and the same threshold works for all alternatives. Choose $P_{\theta_0}(X>k)=\alpha$, giving $k=\theta_0+\log((1-\alpha)/\alpha)$ for 0<α<1. For θ≤θ₀ its rejection probability is at most α. **A**.
questions.theory: Neyman–Pearson compares likelihood ratios for simple hypotheses. A monotone likelihood ratio family yields a common one-sided rejection region for every alternative, giving a uniformly most powerful test by the Karlin–Rubin argument. Size for a composite null is the supremum rejection probability over the null, here attained at θ₀. The logistic CDF is Fθ(x)=s(x−θ). Reversing the alternative reverses the tail. UMP tests for two-sided alternatives generally do not follow from this one-sided argument.

questions.prompt: For the positively oriented circle |z−1|=1, find $(2\pi i)^{-1}\oint dz/(z^3-1)$.

questions.solution: The poles are 1 and ω,ω² with ω=e^(2πi/3). The distances of ω and ω² from the centre 1 are √3>1, so only z=1 is inside. Its residue is 1/(3·1²)=1/3. The residue theorem makes the normalised integral equal to that residue. **B**.
questions.theory: The residue theorem gives a positively oriented contour integral as 2πi times the sum of enclosed residues, weighted by winding numbers for general contours. A simple pole g(z)/h(z) with h(a)=0 and h′(a)≠0 has residue g(a)/h′(a). Poles outside the contour contribute nothing, and a pole on the contour invalidates the ordinary formula. Check geometric location before calculating residues; the contour centre need not be zero.

questions.prompt: For which positive integers p does f(z)=sin z/zᵖ have a holomorphic primitive on C\{0}?
hints: A primitive on the punctured plane exists precisely when the residue at zero vanishes.
Find which term of the sine expansion could produce z⁻¹.
questions.solution: The Laurent expansion is $\sum_{k\ge0}(-1)^k z^{2k+1-p}/(2k+1)!$. A z⁻¹ term requires 2k+1−p=−1, or p=2k+2, an even positive integer. Its coefficient is then nonzero, preventing a primitive. For odd p there is no z⁻¹ term and every Laurent term can be integrated to a single-valued holomorphic function on the punctured plane. Thus **B**.
questions.theory: A holomorphic function has a global primitive exactly when all closed-curve integrals vanish. The punctured plane is not simply connected, and its loop periods are controlled by the residue at the missing point. Integrating z⁻¹ gives a logarithm with nonzero loop period; all other integer Laurent powers have single-valued power primitives. Holomorphicity alone on a multiply connected domain does not ensure a primitive. The residue obstruction is necessary and sufficient here because there is only one puncture and no other singularity.

similar_questions.prompt: Does sin z/z² have a primitive there?
similar_questions.solution: No. Its Laurent series begins 1/z−z/6+⋯, with residue 1.

questions.prompt: Which claim is true for the stated integers?

questions.solution: For even n≥16, the distinct numbers 2 and n/2 appear among 1,…,n−1 and their product is n. Hence n divides (n−1)!, proving **C**. A then has remainder 3 modulo n. B fails at n=17, because none of 1,…,16 contains a factor 17. D fails since n divides n! and therefore n!+1 has remainder 1 even modulo n.
questions.theory: To prove divisibility by a composite number, locate enough prime factors or identify factors whose product equals that number within a larger product. Distinct-factor reasoning must be checked: for n=4 the two proposed factors 2 and n/2 coincide, and 4 does not divide 3!. Universal claims are disproved by a single valid counterexample. Congruences reduce adding small constants to a factorial once its divisibility is known.

questions.prompt: For a nonempty set X, consider intersection and symmetric difference as operations on P(X). Which gives a group?
hints: A△A=∅, and A△∅=A.

questions.solution: Symmetric difference is associative and commutative, has identity ∅, and every set is its own inverse. Thus it is an abelian group. Intersection has identity X, but ∅ cannot have an inverse because ∅∩B=∅≠X for every B. X is nonempty, so intersection is not a group. **C**.
questions.theory: A group requires closure, associativity, an identity, and an inverse for every element. Identify a subset with its 0–1 characteristic function. Symmetric difference becomes coordinatewise addition modulo 2, proving associativity and self-inverse behavior. Intersection becomes coordinatewise multiplication; only the all-one function X is invertible. Together these operations form a Boolean ring, a useful connection between set algebra and algebra over the two-element field.

questions.prompt: Euler’s totient φ(n) counts integers 1≤a≤n coprime to n. Which statement is NOT true?

options.C: Some N>2 satisfies φ(N)<φ(n) for every n>N
options.D: The set {φ(n)/n:n∈N} has finitely many limit points

hints: Use large odd primes to establish rises and falls.
For a fixed prime p, consider φ(pq)/(pq) with varying primes q.
questions.solution: For an odd prime p>3, φ(p)=p−1 while φ(p+1)≤(p+1)/2, so A holds at infinitely many n=p. Also φ(p−1)≤(p−1)/2<p−1=φ(p), proving B at n=p−1. For C choose N=6: φ(6)=2, and φ(n)>2 for n>6. Indeed φ(n) is even for n>2, and φ(n)=2 only for n=3,4,6. For D fix any prime p and let distinct primes q≠p tend to infinity. The distinct ratios φ(pq)/(pq)=(1−1/p)(1−1/q) tend to 1−1/p. Different p give infinitely many distinct limit points, so **D** is false.
questions.theory: Inclusion–exclusion on prime divisors gives φ(n)=n∏ₚ∣ₙ(1−1/p). For even n this is at most n/2. For n>2, residues coprime to n pair as a and n−a without a fixed point, so φ(n) is even. To classify φ(n)=2, each prime divisor p contributes p−1 dividing φ(n), so p is 2 or 3; using φ(2ᵃ3ᵇ) restricts the possibilities to 3,4,6. A limit point of a set requires distinct points approaching it: merely repeating φ(pᵏ)/pᵏ would not suffice. Varying a second prime supplies distinct nearby ratios.

similar_questions.solution: For primes p→∞, the distinct ratios φ(p)/p=1−1/p approach 1.

questions.prompt: A map is closed when it sends every closed set to a closed set. Which claim is true for metric spaces?

options.B: Every product projection onto X is closed
options.C: For continuous f:X→Y and g:Y→Z, if g∘f is closed then g restricted to f(X) is closed
options.D: If f sends closed balls to closed sets then f is closed

hints: For C, take a relatively closed F⊂f(X) and pull it back under f.
Its image under g is exactly the image of f⁻¹(F) under g∘f.
questions.solution: For a closed F in the subspace f(X), continuity of f makes f⁻¹(F) closed in X. Its image under the closed map g∘f is g(F), so g|f(X) is closed. **C**. A fails for (0,1)↪R: the whole subspace is closed in itself but not in R. B fails for the closed hyperbola xy=1 in R², whose projection is R\{0}. D fails for arctan:R→R: images of closed balls are compact intervals, but its whole-domain image is (−π/2,π/2), not closed.
questions.theory: Continuity is defined by closed-set preimages, while closedness concerns images. A relatively closed subset F of a subspace S has the form H∩S for H closed in the ambient space. Product projections are continuous and open, but need not be closed when the other factor is noncompact; a compact other factor does ensure closedness. In R, closed balls are compact, so every continuous map sends them to compact, hence closed, images in a Hausdorff target. This restricted property cannot control arbitrary unbounded closed sets.

similar_questions.prompt: Why is the hyperbola xy=1 closed in R²?
similar_questions.solution: It is the inverse image of the closed singleton {1} under the continuous multiplication map (x,y)↦xy.

similar_questions.prompt: Is a continuous map from a compact space to a Hausdorff space closed?
similar_questions.solution: Yes. Closed subsets of the compact domain are compact; their continuous images are compact and hence closed.
